column2: Elephants, passing other elephants, and horses without riders struck horses; they broke and trampled, Bharata.
Broken and falling, striking one another, they felled others and, having felled them, crushed them.
Senseless, half asleep and veiled in darkness, the men struck down their own, urged on by Time.
Doorkeepers abandoned the gates and guards the posts; they fled as best they could, bewildered, in every direction.
Lost to one another, they did not recognise each other then, lord, crying "Father! Son!", their minds struck by fate.
Fleeing in all directions, abandoning even their own kinsmen, the people then called to one another by clan and name.
Crying "Alas!" others lay on the ground; knowing them, Drona's son, mad for battle, struck them down.
There others, being struck again and again, senseless, kshatriyas tormented by fear, rushed out of the camp.
Weaponless, without armour, hair loosened, with joined palms, trembling, afraid on the ground, the two did not release any.
No one who came out of the camp was released by those two, Kripa and the evil-minded son of Hridika (Kritavarman), great king.
Wishing to do still more for the pleasure of Drona's son, the two set fire to the camp at three places.
Then, in the light of the camp, Ashvatthaman, delight of his father, roamed with his sword like one of practised hand, great king.
The best of the twice-born parted from their lives with his sword some heroes who attacked and others who ran.
Drona's son, valiant, enraged, cutting some warriors in the middle with his sword, felled them like sesame stalks.
The earth was strewn, bull of the Bharatas, with fallen men, horses and the best elephants, crying out and greatly afflicted.
When thousands of men had been slain and fallen, many headless trunks rose up and fell.
He cut off arms with weapons and armlets, and heads, and thighs like elephants' trunks, and hands and feet, Bharata.
Drona's son came upon some cut in the back, some cut in the head, others cut in the side, and some fleeing, and so cut them down.
Others he cut in the middle of the body, others at the ear; striking others at the shoulder he drove the head into the trunk.
As he thus roamed, slaying very many men, the night, with its darkness, appeared dreadful and terrible to behold.
With some still alive and thousands of others slain, and with many elephants and horses, the earth looked terrible.
Thronged with Yakshas and Rakshasas, dreadful with chariots, horses and elephants, those cut down by the enraged Drona's son fell to the earth.
Some cried for their mothers, some for fathers, some for brothers; some said, "This was not done by the enraged Dhritarashtras in the battle.
What was done to us as we slept was done by cruel-deeded Rakshasas; this slaughter of us was done because the Parthas were not present.
The son of Kunti, whose protector is Janardana, cannot be conquered by gods, asuras, Gandharvas, Yakshas or Rakshasas.
Devoted to Brahmanas, truthful, self-controlled, compassionate to all beings, Partha Dhananjaya does not slay one asleep, careless, weaponless, with joined palms, running or with loosened hair.
This dreadful deed has been done to us by the cruel-deeded Rakshasas," lamenting thus many people lay.
After a moment that great tumultuous noise of groaning men and others crying out subsided.
As the earth was drenched with blood, lord of the earth, that dreadful tumultuous dust vanished in a moment.
Enraged, he felled men by thousands, writhing, distraught and spiritless, as the lord of beasts (Rudra) fells beasts.
Embracing one another as they lay, others running, hiding and fighting, Drona's son struck them all down.
Burned by the fire and slain by him, the warriors then sent one another to Yama's abode.
In half of that night, king, Drona's son sent the great army of the Pandavas to Yama's dwelling.
That night, increasing the joy of the night-wandering creatures, was dreadful and exceedingly destructive to men, elephants and horses.
There Rakshasas and Pishachas of various kinds were seen eating human flesh and drinking blood.
Fearful, tawny, dreadful, with teeth like rocks, menstruating, matted, long-thighed, five-footed, big-bellied,
with rough, misshapen fingers behind, of dreadful voices, with pot-like knees, very short, blue-throated, terrifying,
with their children and wives, very cruel, hard to look at and merciless—various forms of Rakshasas were seen there.
Having drunk the blood, they rejoiced and danced in bands; they said, "This is excellent, this is pure, this is sweet."
Very black, eating fat, marrow, bone, blood and rich flesh, those flesh-eaters living on flesh.
Others, having drunk fat, ran about with swollen bellies, with faces of many kinds, dreadful, eating flesh raw.
There were tens of thousands, millions and hundreds of millions of Rakshasas of dreadful form, great and of cruel deeds,
glad and satisfied, at that great slaughter, and many assembled beings, lord of men.
At daybreak he wished to leave the camp; the hilt of Drona's son's sword, drenched in men's blood, had stuck to his hand and become as one with it.
Having left no foe, he shone amid the destruction of the people, like fire at the end of the age, having turned all beings to ashes.
Having done that deed as vowed, Drona's son, lord, having made his father's path hard to reach, was free of fever.
As he had entered the camp at night when the people slept, so he left it, bull among men, after the slaughter, in silence.
Leaving that camp, he met the two, the mighty one, and told them all that deed, glad, delighting them, lord.
They, doing what was pleasing, told him what was pleasing: that thousands of Panchalas and Srinjayas were cut down; and in joy they shouted loudly and clapped their hands.
Such was that very dreadful night for the Somakas, in the destruction of people, asleep and unwary.
Time's course is surely hard to avoid, since such as they were slain after making destruction of our people.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Why did the great chariot-warrior Drona's son not do such a great deed earlier, when my son was set on victory?
And why did that great archer, Drona's son, do this deed after the kshatriyas were slain? You ought to tell me."
[Sanjaya said:] "Surely he did not do it earlier from fear of them, Kuru's delight, because the Parthas and the wise Keshava were absent.
This deed was accomplished by Drona's son also because Satyaki was absent; not even the lord of the Maruts could slay them in their presence.
Such was the event, king, among sleeping people; having made that destruction of the Pandavas' people, the great chariot-warriors met and said to one another, 'By good fortune! By good fortune!'
Then Drona's son embraced them and was congratulated by them, and in joy spoke these supreme words:
'The Panchalas are all slain, the sons of Draupadi in every case, the Somakas and the remnant of the Matsyas are all slain by me.
Now we have done our task; let us go there at once without delay; if our king lives, let us tell him what is pleasing.'"
Going to him, they found the king with a little life left; then, leaping from their chariots, they surrounded your son.
They saw him with broken thighs, lying on the ground, barely alive, senseless, vomiting blood from his mouth.
Surrounded on every side by many terrible beasts, jackals and packs of wolves, ready to devour him close by,
warding off with effort those beasts that wished to eat him, writhing on the ground in severe pain,
the three surviving heroes, afflicted with grief, surrounded the great soul lying on the ground smeared with his own blood: Ashvatthaman, Kripa, and Kritavarman the Satvata.
The king, surrounded by those three great chariot-warriors, smeared with blood and sighing, shone like an altar with three fires.
Seeing the king lying thus, unfit for such a state, those three wept with unbearable grief.
Then, wiping the blood from his mouth with their hands, they piteously lamented the king lying in the battle.

Look at this mace, adorned with gold, golden-hued, of the mace-loving one, fallen on the ground near him.
mahabharata:10:9.12	This mace does not leave the hero in battle after battle; it does not leave the renowned one even as he goes to heaven.
mahabharata:10:9.13	See this gold-adorned mace lying with the hero on his bed, like a loving wife on the bed of dharma.
mahabharata:10:9.14	The scorcher of foes who went at the head of the anointed kings, slain, eats the dust; behold the turning of Time.
mahabharata:10:9.15	He by whom foes were once felled to lie on the ground lies felled on the ground now by his enemies, this king of the Kurus.
mahabharata:10:9.16	He before whom kings bowed in fear by hundreds lies on the hero's bed surrounded by flesh-eaters.
mahabharata:10:9.17	He whom kings once served for wealth, their lord, fie! lies slain suddenly; behold the turning of Time.
[Sanjaya said:] Seeing that best of kings lying there, Ashvatthaman, best of the Bharatas, lamented piteously.

They called you, tiger among kings, the chief of all bowmen, like the lord of wealth in battle, a pupil of Sankarshana.
mahabharata:10:9.20	How, blameless one, did Bhimasena find an opening against you, mighty and skilled as you were, and he the sinful-souled?
mahabharata:10:9.21	Time is surely stronger in this world, great king, if we see you slain in battle by Bhimasena.
mahabharata:10:9.22	How did the petty, sinful, foolish Vrikodara slay you, who know all dharma, by trickery? Surely Time is hard to overcome.
mahabharata:10:9.23	In a righteous fight, called out unrighteously, by Bhimasena with his mace your two thighs were broken.
mahabharata:10:9.24	Fie on Yudhishthira, the petty, who overlooked your head being crushed by a foot after you were slain unrighteously in battle.
mahabharata:10:9.25	Warriors in battles will surely speak ill of Vrikodara as long as beings endure, for you were felled by trickery.
mahabharata:10:9.26	Did not Rama, the delight of the Yadus, always say to you, king: 'There is none equal to Duryodhana with the mace'?
mahabharata:10:9.27	Vrishni praises you, king, in assemblies: 'The Kaurava is my good pupil in mace-fighting,' lord.
mahabharata:10:9.28	The state that great sages call praiseworthy for a kshatriya, slain facing the enemy in battle—you have attained that state.
mahabharata:10:9.29	I do not grieve for you, Duryodhana, bull among men; I grieve for Gandhari, her sons slain, and your father, who will wander as beggars over this earth, grieving.
mahabharata:10:9.30	Fie on Krishna the Vrishni and on ill-minded Arjuna, who think themselves knowers of dharma yet overlooked you being struck down.
mahabharata:10:9.31	And what will all those Pandavas say to the kings, shameless: 'How was Duryodhana slain by us'?
mahabharata:10:9.32	You are fortunate, son of Gandhari, who were slain on the battlefield, going against the enemy in dharma, bull among men.
mahabharata:10:9.33	Gandhari, her sons slain, her kinsmen and relatives slain, and the king whose eye is wisdom, hard to approach, what refuge will they find?
mahabharata:10:9.34	Fie on Kritavarman, on me and on the great chariot-warrior Kripa, that we did not go to heaven, putting you, king, in front,
mahabharata:10:9.35	you, giver of all desires, protector, benefactor of subjects; fie on us, the vilest of men, who do not follow you.
mahabharata:10:9.36	Through your valour, tiger among men, and through Kripa and my father, the houses of us and our servants were full of treasures.
mahabharata:10:9.37	By your grace, we with our friends and kinsmen performed many chief sacrifices with abundant fees.
mahabharata:10:9.38	Where shall we ever find such a company as that with which you went, putting all kings before you?
mahabharata:10:9.39	We three alone, O king, do not follow you as you go to the highest state; for that we shall be tormented.
mahabharata:10:9.40	Deprived of heaven with you, bereft of fortune, remembering your good deeds, what deed could be that we might follow you?
mahabharata:10:9.41	We shall surely wander over this earth in sorrow, best of the Kurus; how, O king, can there be peace or happiness for us bereft of you?
mahabharata:10:9.42	Going there, great king, and meeting those great chariot-warriors, honour them in my name as is fitting, the best and the eldest.
mahabharata:10:9.43	Honouring the teacher, the banner of all bowmen, tell him, king, that Dhrishtadyumna has been slain by me today.
mahabharata:10:9.44	Embrace King Bahlika, the great chariot-warrior, and Saindhava, Somadatta and Bhurishravas,
mahabharata:10:9.45	and the other best kings who have gone before to heaven; embrace them in my words and ask them of their welfare.
Having said this to the king with broken thighs and senseless, Ashvatthaman looked at him and spoke again.

Duryodhana, if you live, hear this word, pleasant to the ear: seven of the Pandavas' side remain, and three of us Dhritarashtras.
mahabharata:10:9.48	Those five brothers and Vasudeva and Satyaki on one side, and I, Kritavarman and Kripa Sharadvata on ours.
mahabharata:10:9.49	The sons of Draupadi are all slain, and the sons of Dhrishtadyumna, the Panchalas are all slain, and the remnant of the Matsyas, Bharata.
mahabharata:10:9.50	See retribution for what was done: the Pandavas have lost their sons; in the Sauptika their camp, with men and mounts, is slain.
mahabharata:10:9.51	And that sinner Dhrishtadyumna, king, was slain by me, entering the camp at night, like a beast.
Hearing that speech, Duryodhana regained his senses with pleasure in his mind and said these words again:

That was not done for me by the son of Ganga, nor Karna, nor your father, what you have done today with Kripa and the Bhoja (Kritavarman).
mahabharata:10:9.54	If that petty general (Dhrishtadyumna) is slain together with Shikhandin, then I think myself today equal to Maghavan (Indra).
mahabharata:10:9.55	Good fortune to you; may you prosper; we shall meet again in heaven. Having said this, the great-minded king of the Kurus fell silent and gave up his life, leaving his friends in grief.
They embraced the king, saying "So be it," and, looking at him again and again, mounted their own chariots.
Hearing thus the piteous words of your son, at daybreak, afflicted with grief, I ran to the city.
When your son went to heaven, blameless one, the divine sight given me by the sage was lost to me today, as I was struck with grief.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing this, the king, sighing long and hot over the slaying of his sons and kinsmen, then fell into thought.

The sons of Draupadi, great king, with the sons of Drupada, careless and trusting at night, were sleeping in their own camp.
mahabharata:10:10.3	Your camp was slain at night by the cruel Kritavarman, Gautama (Kripa) and the sinful Ashvatthaman.
mahabharata:10:10.4	By those, cutting down thousands of men, elephants and horses with lances, spears and axes, your host was left without remainder.
mahabharata:10:10.5	Like a great forest being cut by axes, a very great sound of your army was heard, Bharata.
mahabharata:10:10.6	I alone remain, king, from that army, freed somehow, righteous one, while Kritavarman was occupied.
Hearing that inauspicious speech, Yudhishthira, son of Kunti, the invincible, fell to the earth, overcome with grief for his sons.
As he fell, Satyaki rushed and caught him, and Bhimasena, Arjuna and the two Pandavas, sons of Madri.
Regaining consciousness, the son of Kunti, with a voice distraught with grief, lamented in distress: "Having conquered the foes, I am afterwards conquered."

Abandoning whom, the ill-minded one later suffers as if fallen into calamity; he would consider his victory worthless, being then conquered more by his enemies.
mahabharata:10:10.14	For whose sake—fie on the victory of the sinful—the friends are slain; the victors, overcome by the careful vanquished, are conquered.
mahabharata:10:10.15	Those who in the battle were spared through Karna's carelessness, of the one with arrow-teeth, sword-tongue, bow-mouth, terrible, roaring with the twang of the bowstring,
mahabharata:10:10.16	the enraged lion among men, who never fled in battle—these have been slain.
mahabharata:10:10.17	The lake of chariots, with waves of arrow-showers, adorned with jewels, with rows of vehicles, with fish of spears and lances, banners and elephant-crocodiles, the whirlpool of bows with arrows for foam,
mahabharata:10:10.18	the shore swelling with the moonrise of battle, the Drona ocean with the sound of the bowstring as its rim—those who crossed it in boats of weapons high and low, those princes have been slain by carelessness.
mahabharata:10:10.19	For there is no greater death for men in this world of the living than carelessness; wealth abandons the careless man on all sides, and misfortunes enter.
mahabharata:10:10.20	The best of banners as the lofty comet, arrows as flames, anger as the great wind, the great bow with the twang of the string as its rim, armour and various weapons as the oblations,
mahabharata:10:10.21	the great-forest-like great army, Bhishma the great forest fire in the great battle—those who bore the force of raised weapons, those princes have been slain by carelessness.
mahabharata:10:10.22	A careless man cannot win learning, austerity, glory or vast fortune; see how, by carelessness, all enemies being slain, Mahendra prospers in happiness.
mahabharata:10:10.23	See the sons and grandsons of kings, like Indra, slain alike by carelessness; like rich merchants who crossed the ocean and sank in a small river, careless. Those slain by the intolerant as they lay, without doubt, have gone to heaven.
mahabharata:10:10.24	I grieve for Krishna, the virtuous: how will she not perish in an ocean of grief, hearing of her brothers and sons slain, the Panchala king, her father, and her aged one? Surely she will fall senseless to the ground, her slender frame wasted by grief.
mahabharata:10:10.25	How, unable to bear that grief born of sorrow, will she, accustomed to happiness, live, driven by the slaying of her sons and brothers, as if burning in fire?
Lamenting thus in distress, the king of the Kurus said to Nakula: "Go, bring here this unfortunate princess with her mother's side."
Taking the words of the king, like dharma itself in dharma, the son of Madri went by chariot swiftly to the dwelling of the queen, where were the wives of the Panchala king.
Having sent Madri's son, the descendant of Ajamidha, afflicted with grief, went with his friends, weeping, to the battlefield of his sons, thronged with hosts of spirits.
Entering that inauspicious, fierce place, he saw his sons, friends and companions lying on the ground, their bodies wet with blood, their heads split, broken and carried off.
Seeing them, Yudhishthira, best of upholders of dharma, in great distress cried out loudly, the foremost Kaurava, and fell to the ground senseless with his companions.
Then great grief arose in that great soul, remembering his sons, grandsons, brothers and kin.
Seeing him with eyes full of tears, trembling and senseless, his friends, greatly agitated, consoled him then.
Then at that moment Nakula came in a chariot of sunlike radiance with Krishna (Draupadi), who was in extreme distress.
She had gone to Upaplavya, and hearing then the very unpleasant news of the destruction of all her sons, she was greatly pained.
Like a plantain tree trembling, shaken by the wind, Krishna, reaching the king, afflicted with grief, fell to the ground.
Her face, of the lotus-petal-eyed one, suddenly became wasted by grief, like the sun veiled in darkness.
Seeing her fallen, the truly valiant Vrikodara, in agitation, came up and caught her with both arms.
Comforted by Bhimasena, the lady Krishna, weeping, said to the Pandava, with his brother:

Hearing that your heroic sons were felled by that dharma, you will by good fortune not remember me at Upaplavya.
mahabharata:10:11.13	Hearing of the slaying of the sleeping by sinful Drona's son, grief burns me, Partha, like a fire in a hollow.
mahabharata:10:11.14	If today in battle that sinner Drona's son, with his followers, does not have his life taken by you in valiant fight,
mahabharata:10:11.15	I shall sit here to fast to death; know that, Pandavas, if Drona's son does not gain the fruit of his sinful deed.
Having said this, Krishna, the renowned Yajnaseni, sat down before the Pandava Yudhishthira, the king of dharma.
Seeing his beloved queen seated, the Pandava royal sage, righteous, said to the fair-looking Draupadi:

Your sons and brothers, auspicious one, knower of dharma, have obtained a righteous death by dharma; you ought not to grieve for them.
mahabharata:10:11.19	That Drona's son, auspicious one, has gone far away to the forest; how will you know his felling in battle, fair one?

[Draupadi said:] "I have heard that Drona's son has a jewel born with him on his head; having slain that sinner in battle, I would see the jewel brought; placing it on your head, O king, I would live—that is my resolve."
[Vaishampayana said:] Having said this to the Pandava king, fair-looking Krishna, angry, went to Bhimasena and said:

Bhima, remembering the kshatriya dharma, you ought to save me; slay that sinner as Maghavan slew Shambara. There is no man in the world equal to you in valour.
mahabharata:10:11.23	It is heard in all the worlds how in the great calamity you were an island for the Parthas in the city of Varanavata and at the sight of Hidimba, and then you were the refuge.
mahabharata:10:11.24	So too in the city of Virata, when I was sorely oppressed by Kichaka, you rescued me from the difficulty as Maghavan rescued Paulomi.
mahabharata:10:11.25	As you did these great deeds of old, Partha, so slay Drona's son, slayer of foes, and be happy.
Hearing her manifold lament of grief, the mighty son of Kunti, Bhimasena, could not bear it.
He mounted a great golden-ornamented chariot, taking a splendid, wondrous bow with its string and arrows.
Making Nakula his charioteer, set on the slaying of Drona's son, he stretched his bow with its arrow and quickly urged on the horses.
Those horses, tiger among men, urged on, swift as the wind, went hastily with speed, fast-going bays.
Taking up the tracks of the chariot from the camp, the unfallen, valiant one quickly went along the road of Drona's son's chariot.
This is your brother the Pandava, unable to bear his grief for his sons, going into the fray to slay Drona's son, Bharata.
Thousands of causes of grief and hundreds of causes of fear enter the fool day after day, not the wise man.
That boy, endowed with splendour, came to be called a charioteer's son and learned archery from your teacher, the best of the Angirases.
Moving and unmoving beings, in heaven or on earth, all are of the nature of Time; this world has the nature of the serpent Time.
Sacrifice with the Ashvamedha, duly with fees, and give many desired things and wealth, as Rama son of Dasharatha did.
Gandhari and Vidura were pleased by the king's steadiness, and by the purity of Ajatashatru, but not, slayer of foes, by Bhima's.
Having said this, Vasudeva, wishing to make it true, then ordered a pilgrimage, subduer of foes.
[Yudhishthira said:] "She had great partiality, especially for Dhananjaya; this is its fruit, best of men, that she enjoys today."
Hot sands of the Karambha, separate iron rocks, and iron pots of oil boiling all around.
